title: Loom Recording Not Uploading: How to Fix It
body_md:
![support.atlassian.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/loom-recording-not-uploading-how-to-fix-it/1.png)
*Screenshot of support.atlassian.com ([source](https://support.atlassian.com/loom/kb/troubleshoot-a-video-stuck-in-processing/))*

First wait at least 30 minutes and keep the recording tab or app open. For a desktop recording that remains stuck, follow [Loom's recovery guidance](https://support.atlassian.com/loom/kb/troubleshoot-a-video-stuck-in-processing/): reboot the desktop app, give it a few minutes to process and refresh the video link, or visit the recovery module. Loom says it has no recovery method for Chrome extension or mobile recordings, so don't toggle, remove or reinstall the extension while a recording is still uploading.

Before you panic: a video that's still spinning isn't necessarily lost. Loom's own doc tells you to wait at least 30 minutes and only start troubleshooting after that.

Long recordings on a slow connection legitimately take longer, because Loom is still finishing the upload while the status says "processing."

## Why This Happens

![support.atlassian.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/loom-recording-not-uploading-how-to-fix-it/2.png)
*Screenshot of support.atlassian.com ([source](https://support.atlassian.com/loom/kb/troubleshoot-and-fix-loom-video-upload-failures/))*

A Loom video isn't saved until it's been shipped to Loom's servers and transcoded. Anything that breaks that handoff leaves you staring at a stuck upload. The usual suspects, per Loom's docs:

- **A network hiccup mid-recording or mid-upload.** An interruption while recording or during processing — a Wi-Fi or internet dropout — can stop the video uploading successfully.
- **Slow upload speed.** Loom recommends at least 5 Mbps upload. Home connections are often asymmetrical, so your fast download number tells you nothing.
- **The app crashed.** A crash can leave files that never upload.
- **Length and quality.** Longer videos take longer, and higher recording resolutions take longer still. For reference, Loom says a sub-10-minute 720p video shouldn't take more than a few minutes on a strong connection.
- **Several videos in the queue.** Multiple videos processing at once is on the same list.
- **File limits, if you're uploading an existing video rather than recording one.** A "Failed to process" message most often means the file is over 4 GB, over 60 fps, or above 4096 x 2160, and uploads are capped at 4 GB or 12 hours, whichever is less.
- **Corporate VPNs, proxies, and security software** that inspect or throttle large outbound uploads.

## Step-by-Step Fixes

![support.atlassian.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/loom-recording-not-uploading-how-to-fix-it/3.png)
*Screenshot of support.atlassian.com ([source](https://support.atlassian.com/loom/kb/fix-loom-videos-that-wont-play-or-load-desktop-app-only/))*

### 1. Wait out the 30-minute window

Boring, but it saves a lot of unnecessary work. Loom sets the troubleshooting threshold at 30 minutes without processing. Keep the app or tab open while you wait — Loom says not to close the tab until you can play the video.

### 2. Restart the recorder you used

**Desktop app:** quit Loom completely (don't just close the window — use the menu bar or system tray icon), reopen it, and let it resume. Loom's official fix for desktop videos that won't load is the Recovery Page plus restarting the desktop app.

**Chrome extension:** open Chrome's Extensions > Manage Extensions, turn the Loom extension off and back on, then wait a few minutes and refresh the link.

### 3. Check your actual upload speed

Run a speed test and look at upload speed, not download speed. Loom wants at least 5 Mbps up and points you at speedtest.net. A slow or restricted network may be the problem, but don't assume a particular Wi-Fi location or VPN is the cause. Try a stable authorised connection. Don't disable an employer-required VPN or security tool without permission.

### 4. Use Loom's recovery page

If the video is still stuck or missing from your library, go to **loom.com/recover-videos**. One important caveat: the recovery page only works for videos you own that were recorded with the Loom desktop app (screen only or screen + cam). Loom states it has no recovery method for Chrome extension or mobile recordings at the moment.

### 5. Hunt for local video parts (desktop app only)

If the video still fails after restarting the app, check local storage for unsaved video parts — Loom has separate instructions for the Mac and Windows apps — and if parts are found, send them to Support, who can sometimes manually repair the recording. Do this sooner rather than later: Loom notes that a video not processed successfully after 24 hours gets filtered out of your dashboard view.

### 6. Reset the extension or update your software

Loom's extension guide puts "remove the extension at chrome://extensions/, restart the browser, log in, reinstall" last, as the step to try if issues persist — not something to do while a video is mid-upload. Save it for when nothing is recording or processing.

The same guide also says to check for a Chrome update at chrome://settings/help and restart Chrome afterwards. On the desktop app, check for an app update too.

### 7. Re-encode the file (uploads, not recordings)

If you're uploading an existing MP4 and hitting "Failed to process," check it against Loom's limits first. If the file isn't supported, or you think it should be and it's being rejected anyway, Loom suggests running it through HandBrake — sometimes an underlying property is the real blocker and re-encoding is the only fix.

### 8. Contact support

If local parts exist and nothing else worked, open a ticket and attach them. That's the path Loom itself points to for manual repair.

## How to Prevent It Next Time

![support.atlassian.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/loom-recording-not-uploading-how-to-fix-it/4.png)
*Screenshot of support.atlassian.com ([source](https://support.atlassian.com/loom/kb/quickly-fix-common-recording-errors/))*

- **Don't close the app or tab until the video plays.** That's Loom's instruction, not a superstition.
- **Use the desktop app for anything important.** It's the only recorder with an official recovery path. Loom also recommends the desktop app when Chrome is under heavy load, since it uses your system's resources instead of sharing Chrome's RAM.
- **Record at a lower resolution** for long videos. Higher recording quality means longer processing.
- **Break long recordings into chunks.** A 5-minute clip that uploads beats a 45-minute one that stalls — and people watch short Looms anyway.
- **Upload one at a time.** Multiple videos processing simultaneously is a documented cause of delays.
- **Get on a stable connection before you hit record,** and drop the VPN if your company allows it. Closing unnecessary tabs and background apps to free up resources is also on Loom's list.

*Updated October 2026: this guide is built from Loom's current Atlassian support documentation, not from a controlled diagnostic test.*

## My Take

I think the single most useful thing in all of this is the split between recorders. The desktop app has a recovery page and local video parts you can mail to support; the Chrome extension and mobile apps have, by Loom's own admission, nothing. If a recording would be painful to redo, that decision gets made before you press record, not after the spinner hangs.

My read on the 30-minute rule is that it's mostly honest. "Processing" in Loom often means "still uploading," so a long 1080p recording on a weak connection is slow for reasons that have nothing to do with a bug. The frustrating part is the UI doesn't distinguish between the two, which is why people start reinstalling extensions and destroy a video that would have landed on its own.

To be fair to Loom, almost every cloud recorder has this shape of failure, and the docs are unusually specific — exact limits, an exact speed target, platform-specific instructions for finding local parts. That's better than most vendors do.

Still, the practical advice I'd give is unglamorous: desktop app, shorter takes, 720p or 1080p, one upload at a time, and don't close anything until the video actually plays. And if the recording matters legally or financially — a client deliverable, a compliance walkthrough — I'm not a lawyer or a compliance professional, so treat a second local capture as cheap insurance rather than taking my word on what's safe to rely on.
